text: Last lesson gave you the theory — bias, variance, and generalization. This lesson turns it into a practical skill. When a model disappoints, you should be able to look at two numbers, its score on training data and its score on held-out data, and say which problem you have and what to try next.

A simple diagnosis table. Poor training and poor held-out scores, similar to each other, means underfitting — high bias, model too simple. Excellent training but much worse held-out means overfitting — high variance, the model memorized. Good training with a similar, slightly lower held-out score means a good fit. The size of the gap tells you about variance; the level of both tells you about bias.

Using scikit-learn's make_moons, two interleaving half-circles with real overlap so no model can be perfect, and a decision tree whose max_depth controls flexibility directly. Sweeping depth from 1 to 15 and recording train and held-out accuracy at each setting.

Depth 1 scores about 80 percent on both sets — poor on training data itself means the model can't even fit what it sees, that's underfitting. Depths 2 to 4 reach held-out accuracy around 91 percent with the training score close behind — the sweet spot.

Depth 15 memorizes the training set completely, 100 percent, but scores only 85.6 percent on held-out rows — a gap of nearly 15 points, that's overfitting. Notice the training score only ever rises — if you tuned on training accuracy alone, you'd always pick the deepest tree. Only the held-out curve turns back downward.

If you're underfitting, both scores poor: use a more flexible model, add informative features or interactions, or reduce regularization if you're using any. If you're overfitting, a big gap: constrain the model, limit depth or add regularization, get more data if you can, remove noisy features, or use an ensemble like a random forest that averages away variance.

Holding the unlimited tree back to max_depth equals 3 lifts held-out accuracy from 0.856 to 0.906. A min_samples_leaf setting of 15 closed the training-test gap but didn't actually improve the score here — a reminder that fixes need testing, not assuming. And with only 160 held-out rows, differences of a point or two are genuinely noise.

One caution: we chose the best depth by peeking at held-out accuracy, which makes that 0.906 slightly optimistic, since we picked the winner from many candidates on the same rows. The real fix, coming in lesson 7, is a three-way split — train, validation for choosing settings, and a test set used exactly once. To recap: compare training and held-out scores, diagnose underfitting or overfitting, and always confirm on a set you never touched. Next up, lesson 6: loss functions and optimization.
